skills: Area and perimeter of plane figures
Volume and surface area of solids

lesson.intro: Every formula this topic needs is printed on the reference sheet the Digital SAT gives you. That is exactly why the questions are never "do you remember the formula?" They are "which quantity in this sentence is the radius, which is the height, and what am I actually being asked for?" The three things the test really measures are: picking the right relationship, running it backwards when the area or volume is the number you are given, and knowing what happens to area and volume when every length in a figure is multiplied by the same factor.

blocks.title: Plane figures: area and perimeter
blocks.body: Perimeter is a length: add up the outside edges, and it is measured in inches, cm, feet. Area is a covering: it is measured in \emph{square} units. A question that asks for fencing, trim, ribbon, or the distance around a track wants perimeter; a question that asks for carpet, paint, sod, or glass wants area. Reading which one is being asked for is worth more points on this topic than any algebra.

blocks.title: The plane-figure formulas
blocks.body: Rectangle: $A=\ell w$, $P=2\ell+2w$. \\ Triangle: $A=\frac{1}{2}bh$. \\ Parallelogram: $A=bh$. \\ Trapezoid: $A=\frac{1}{2}(b_1+b_2)h$. \\ Circle of radius $r$: $A=\pi r^2$, $C=2\pi r=\pi d$. \\ In every one of these, $h$ means the \emph{perpendicular} height, not the length of a slanted side.

blocks.title: One idea behind four formulas
blocks.body: A parallelogram is a rectangle with a triangle slid from one end to the other, so its area is still $bh$. A triangle is half of a parallelogram, so it is $\frac{1}{2}bh$. A trapezoid is a parallelogram whose base is the \emph{average} of the two parallel sides, so it is $\frac{b_1+b_2}{2}\cdot h$. If you can see the figure as base times perpendicular height, you can rebuild any of them.

blocks.title: Solids: volume and surface area
blocks.body: Volume is how much a solid holds, in cubic units. Surface area is how much material wraps around it, in square units. For any prism or cylinder, volume is $(\text{area of the base})\times(\text{height})$ --- that single sentence covers boxes, triangular prisms and cylinders at once. Cones and pyramids are the same base and height, taken one third of the way: exactly one third of the prism or cylinder that would enclose them.

blocks.title: The solids on the reference sheet
blocks.body: Rectangular box: $V=\ell wh$, $SA=2(\ell w+\ell h+wh)$. \\ Prism or cylinder: $V=Bh$; cylinder $V=\pi r^2h$, lateral area $2\pi rh$, total surface area $2\pi r^2+2\pi rh$. \\ Cone: $V=\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2h$. Pyramid: $V=\frac{1}{3}Bh$. \\ Sphere: $V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, $SA=4\pi r^2$.

blocks.title: Radius, diameter, and slant height
blocks.body: Three misreadings account for most lost points here. (1) A problem that hands you a \emph{diameter} of $16$ and a formula that wants $r$: using $16$ as the radius multiplies a circle's area by $4$. (2) The \emph{slant height} of a cone or pyramid is the distance up the sloped surface, not the vertical height; you must use the Pythagorean theorem to get the real height first. (3) Dropping the $\frac{1}{3}$ in a cone or pyramid triples the answer, and the tripled value is always sitting there among the choices.

blocks.title: Working backwards from an area or a volume
blocks.body: When the question gives you the area or volume and asks for a length, do not hunt for a different formula. Write the same formula, put the unknown in as a letter, set it equal to the number you were given, and solve. \emph{A cylinder holds $100\pi$ and is $4$ tall}: write $\pi r^2(4)=100\pi$, divide by $4\pi$ to get $r^2=25$, so $r=5$. Then --- and this is where points are lost --- reread the question, because it often wants something built from that length, such as the surface area, not the length itself.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: a composite figure
blocks.body: \textbf{A running-track infield is a $20$ m by $10$ m rectangle with a semicircle attached to each of the two short ends. What is its area?} \\ Cut it into pieces you have formulas for. The rectangle contributes $20\cdot 10=200$ square metres. Each short end is $10$ m long, so each semicircle has \emph{diameter} $10$ and therefore radius $5$ --- this is the step the test is testing. The two semicircles together make one full circle of radius $5$, area $\pi(5)^2=25\pi$. Total: $200+25\pi$ square metres. Note what would have happened had you called the radius $10$: you would get $200+100\pi$, which is one of the choices every time.

blocks.title: Scaling: the $k$, $k^2$, $k^3$ law
blocks.body: Suppose every length in a figure is multiplied by the same factor $k$. Then every length --- side, perimeter, radius, circumference, diagonal --- is multiplied by $k$; every area --- the figure's area, a solid's surface area --- is multiplied by $k^2$; and every volume is multiplied by $k^3$. This one sentence is the source of most hard questions in this topic.

blocks.title: Why the exponents are 1, 2 and 3
blocks.body: Look at the formulas. A rectangle's area is $\ell w$: scale both lengths by $k$ and you get $(k\ell)(kw)=k^2\ell w$. A circle's area is $\pi r^2$: replacing $r$ with $kr$ gives $\pi k^2r^2$. A box's volume is $\ell wh$: three lengths scaled means $k^3$. Every area formula multiplies exactly two lengths and every volume formula exactly three, so the exponent counts the dimensions.

blocks.title: Scaling by $k$ when you should scale by $k^2$
blocks.body: \emph{A photo's dimensions are each multiplied by $3$; its area was $12$ square inches, so the new area is $36$.} That is the single most common wrong answer on the test, and it is wrong: the new area is $12\cdot 3^2=108$. Run the law backwards too. If a volume grows by a factor of $27$, the lengths grew by $\sqrt[3]{27}=3$, and so the surface area grew by $3^2=9$ --- not by $27$.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: scaling in reverse
blocks.body: \textbf{Two similar cones have volumes $27$ cm$^3$ and $125$ cm$^3$. The smaller cone's base radius is $6$ cm. What is the larger cone's base radius?} \\ Similar means one is a scale copy of the other, so some factor $k$ multiplies every length. Volumes are in the ratio $k^3$, and $\dfrac{125}{27}=k^3$, so $k=\sqrt[3]{125/27}=\dfrac{5}{3}$. Radii are lengths, so they scale by $k$, not by $k^3$: the larger radius is $6\cdot\dfrac{5}{3}=10$ cm. Cube-rooting the volume ratio first, then applying the plain factor to a length, is the whole method.

blocks.title: A four-line checklist
blocks.body: 1. Circle the words \emph{perimeter}, \emph{area}, \emph{volume}, \emph{surface area} in the question, and check the units in the answer choices --- square or cubic. 2. Label the figure with every number in the text and ask of each: is that a radius or a diameter, a height or a slant height? 3. If the given number \emph{is} the area or volume, set the formula equal to it and solve for the letter. 4. If nothing is numeric and lengths are being multiplied, it is the $k$, $k^2$, $k^3$ question.

problems.stem: A rectangular tabletop is $12$ inches long and $7$ inches wide. What is the area, in square inches, of the tabletop?
steps: Area of a rectangle is $A=\ell w$.
problems.solution: Area multiplies the two dimensions; adding them ($19$) or doubling that sum ($38$, the perimeter) answers a different question. The answer is $84$ square inches.

problems.stem: A triangle has a base of length $10$ centimeters and a height of $6$ centimeters. What is the area, in square centimeters, of the triangle?
problems.solution: A triangle is half of the parallelogram with the same base and height, so the $\frac{1}{2}$ is not optional: $10\cdot 6=60$ is the parallelogram's area, and the triangle's is $30$ square centimeters.

problems.stem: A circle has a radius of $5$ inches. What is the area, in square inches, of the circle?
problems.solution: Squaring the radius is what makes the answer an area. Here $10\pi$ is the circumference and $100\pi$ is what you get by using the diameter $10$ in place of the radius, so the area is $25\pi$ square inches.

problems.stem: A rectangular box has a length of $9$ inches, a width of $5$ inches, and a height of $4$ inches. What is the volume, in cubic inches, of the box?
problems.solution: The volume of any prism is the area of its base times its height: the base here is $9\cdot 5=45$ square inches, and stacking that base through $4$ inches of height gives $180$ cubic inches.

problems.stem: A circular garden has a diameter of $14$ feet. What is the circumference, in feet, of the garden?
problems.solution: Because the diameter is given directly, use $C=\pi d$ rather than $C=2\pi r$; treating $14$ as the radius doubles the answer to $28\pi$, and squaring the radius gives the area $49\pi$. The circumference is $14\pi$ feet.

problems.figure: \begin{center}\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.42,line join=round] \draw[thick,satnavy] (0,0)--(9,0)--(11,4)--(2,4)--cycle; \draw[dashed,satgrey] (9,0)--(9,4); \draw[satgrey] (9,0.5)--(8.5,0.5)--(8.5,0); \node[below] at (4.5,0) {$9$}; \node[right] at (9,2) {$4$}; \end{tikzpicture}\end{center}\satnote{Figure not drawn to scale.}
problems.stem: In the parallelogram shown, the base has length $9$ and the height is $4$. What is the area of the parallelogram?
problems.solution: A parallelogram is a rectangle with one corner triangle slid across, so no factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ appears; halving would give $18$, which is the area of a triangle with this base and height. The area is $36$.

problems.stem: A cube has edges of length $4$ centimeters. What is the surface area, in square centimeters, of the cube?
steps: A cube has $6$ congruent square faces.
problems.solution: Surface area counts material, so add up all six faces rather than multiplying the three dimensions (that would give the volume, $64$). The surface area is $96$ square centimeters.

problems.stem: The trapezoid shown has parallel sides of length $8$ and $12$ and a height of $5$. What is the area of the trapezoid?
problems.solution: A trapezoid behaves like a parallelogram whose base is the average of the two parallel sides, $\frac{8+12}{2}=10$, so the area is $10\cdot 5=50$. Using one base alone gives $40$ or $60$, and forgetting the $\frac{1}{2}$ gives $100$.

problems.stem: A cylindrical can has a radius of $3$ inches and a height of $10$ inches. What is the volume, in cubic inches, of the can?
steps: The base is a circle of area $\pi(3)^2=9\pi$.
problems.solution: Volume of a cylinder is base area times height, so the radius must be squared: $30\pi$ comes from forgetting to square it, $60\pi$ is the lateral surface area $2\pi rh$, and $360\pi$ comes from using the diameter $6$ as the radius. The volume is $90\pi$ cubic inches.

problems.stem: A right circular cone has a base radius of $6$ centimeters and a height of $10$ centimeters. What is the volume, in cubic centimeters, of the cone?
problems.solution: A cone fills exactly one third of the cylinder with the same base and height, and that cylinder holds $360\pi$; dropping the $\frac{1}{3}$ gives $360\pi$ and using $\frac{1}{2}$ gives $180\pi$. The volume is $120\pi$ cubic centimeters.

problems.stem: A triangle has an area of $84$ square units and a base of length $24$ units. What is the length of the height drawn to that base?
problems.solution: When the area is the number you are given, put the unknown into the same formula and solve rather than looking for a new one: $\frac{1}{2}bh=84$ with $b=24$ gives $h=7$ units.

problems.stem: In the figure shown, every angle is a right angle. What is the area of the region?
steps: Complete the shape to a $10$ by $6$ rectangle, area $60$.
The missing corner is $4$ by $3$, area $12$.
problems.solution: A composite figure should be cut into rectangles or completed to one; here the whole rectangle is $60$ and the notch removes $12$, so the region is $48$. Splitting instead into a $6\times 6$ square and a $4\times 3$ rectangle gives $36+12=48$ as well.

problems.stem: Rectangle $B$ is formed by multiplying both the length and the width of rectangle $A$ by $3$. The area of rectangle $B$ is how many times the area of rectangle $A$?
steps: If $A$ has area $\ell w$, then $B$ has area $(3\ell)(3w)$.
problems.solution: Area multiplies two lengths, so a scale factor of $3$ appears twice: the area is multiplied by $3^2=9$, not by $3$. The factor $27=3^3$ would apply to a volume, where three lengths are multiplied.

problems.stem: A sphere has a radius of $3$ inches. What is the volume, in cubic inches, of the sphere?
problems.solution: Cube the radius first, then take $\frac{4}{3}$ of it: $4\pi(27)=108\pi$ drops the division by $3$, and $288\pi$ comes from using the diameter $6$ as the radius. The volume is $36\pi$ cubic inches.

problems.stem: A right circular cylinder has a volume of $100\pi$ cubic centimeters and a height of $4$ centimeters. What is the radius, in centimeters, of the cylinder's base?
problems.solution: Set the volume formula equal to the given volume and solve for the letter; dividing by $\pi$ first clears it from the problem entirely, leaving $r^2=25$, so the radius is $5$ centimeters.
problems.verify:
r = symbols('r', positive=True)
result = solve(Eq(pi*r**2*4, 100*pi), r)[0]

problems.stem: The radius of a right circular cone is multiplied by $2$ and its height is multiplied by $3$. The volume of the new cone is how many times the volume of the original cone?
problems.solution: This is not the uniform-scaling law, because the two dimensions grow by different factors, so substitute directly: the radius is squared in the formula and so contributes $2^2=4$, while the height contributes $3$, for a total factor of $12$. Multiplying the factors as $2\cdot 3=6$ ignores the square.

problems.figure: \begin{center}\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.34,line join=round] \draw[thick,satnavy] (0,0) ellipse (5 and 1.3); \draw[thick,satnavy] (-5,0)--(0,7)--(5,0); \draw[dashed,satgrey] (0,0)--(5,0); \node[below] at (2.5,-0.1) {$5$}; \node[right] at (3,4) {$13$}; \end{tikzpicture}\end{center}\satnote{Figure not drawn to scale.}
problems.stem: A right circular cone has a base radius of $5$ and a slant height of $13$, as shown. What is the volume of the cone?
steps: The radius, the height and the slant height form a right triangle: $5^2+h^2=13^2$.
problems.solution: The slant height runs up the sloped surface, so it is the hypotenuse, never the height in the volume formula; using $13$ directly produces $\frac{325\pi}{3}$. Finding $h=12$ from the $5$-$12$-$13$ triangle first gives the volume $100\pi$.

problems.stem: A rectangular prism with a square base has a volume of $500$ cubic inches and a height of $5$ inches. What is the surface area, in square inches, of the prism?
steps: Let the base edge be $s$: $s^2(5)=500$, so $s^2=100$ and $s=10$.
problems.solution: Work backwards from the volume to the missing length, then reread the question, which asks for surface area rather than that length. Counting only the four sides gives $200$ and adding just one base gives $300$; the full surface area is $400$ square inches.
problems.verify:
s = symbols('s', positive=True)
ss = solve(Eq(s**2*5, 500), s)[0]
result = 2*ss**2 + 4*ss*5

problems.stem: A sculptor builds a scale model of a statue. Every length on the statue is $4$ times the corresponding length on the model. The model has a total surface area of $25$ square inches. What is the total surface area, in square inches, of the statue?
problems.solution: Surface area is an area, so the scale factor enters squared: multiplying by $4$ instead of $16$ is the classic error. The statue's surface area is $400$ square inches.

problems.stem: A cylindrical tank with a base radius of $4$ feet and a height of $9$ feet is filled with water to $\frac{2}{3}$ of its capacity. What is the volume, in cubic feet, of the water in the tank?
problems.solution: Find the whole first and take the fraction of it at the end; $144\pi$ is the full tank and $48\pi$ is the empty third. Using the diameter $8$ as the radius would give $384\pi$. The water occupies $96\pi$ cubic feet.

problems.stem: A trapezoid has an area of $60$ square units and a height of $6$ units. One of its parallel sides is $3$ times as long as the other. What is the length of the longer parallel side?
steps: Let the shorter side be $x$, so the longer is $3x$.
problems.solution: Naming the shorter side $x$ turns the sentence into one equation in one unknown; the trap is stopping at $x=5$, which is the shorter side. The longer parallel side is $15$ units.

problems.stem: The volume of a sphere is $27$ times the volume of a smaller sphere. The surface area of the larger sphere is how many times the surface area of the smaller sphere?
problems.solution: Run the scaling law backwards: the volume ratio gives the length ratio only after a cube root, and that length ratio is then squared for the surface area. Reusing $27$ for the area is the intended error; the answer is $9$.

problems.stem: A square has an area of $144$ square meters. What is the perimeter, in meters, of the square?
problems.solution: The square root of the area is the side, and the question asks for the distance around, which is four of those sides. Stopping at $s=12$ gives the first choice; the perimeter is $48$ meters.
problems.verify:
s = symbols('s', positive=True)
ss = solve(Eq(s**2, 144), s)[0]
result = 4*ss

problems.stem: A circle has an area of $49\pi$ square centimeters. What is the circumference, in centimeters, of the circle?
problems.solution: Cancel the $\pi$ on both sides to recover the radius, then use it in the circumference formula; using $49$ itself as the radius produces $98\pi$. The circumference is $14\pi$ centimeters.
problems.verify:
r = symbols('r', positive=True)
rr = solve(Eq(pi*r**2, 49*pi), r)[0]
result = 2*pi*rr

problems.stem: A rectangular box has a volume of $240$ cubic inches. The base of the box measures $8$ inches by $6$ inches. What is the height, in inches, of the box?
steps: The base area is $8\cdot 6=48$ square inches.
problems.solution: Volume is base area times height, so divide by the whole base area, not by a single edge: dividing by $8$ gives $30$ and by $6$ gives $40$. The height is $5$ inches.
problems.verify:
h = symbols('h', positive=True)
result = solve(Eq(8*6*h, 240), h)[0]

problems.stem: A cube has a volume of $125$ cubic centimeters. What is the surface area, in square centimeters, of the cube?
steps: Each of the $6$ faces has area $25$.
problems.solution: Take the cube root of the volume to get the edge, then build the surface area from that edge; the volume and the surface area are different measurements of the same cube. The surface area is $150$ square centimeters.
problems.verify:
s = symbols('s', positive=True)
ss = solve(Eq(s**3, 125), s)[0]
result = 6*ss**2

problems.stem: A circular pizza has a diameter of $16$ inches. What is the area, in square inches, of the pizza?
problems.solution: The area formula needs the radius, so halve the diameter before squaring; using $16$ as the radius gives $256\pi$, four times too large. The area is $64\pi$ square inches.

problems.stem: Each edge of a cube is multiplied by $4$ to produce a larger cube. The volume of the larger cube is how many times the volume of the original cube?
problems.solution: Volume multiplies three lengths, so the scale factor appears three times: $4^3=64$. The choice $16$ is the factor for surface area and $12$ comes from multiplying $4$ by the three dimensions instead of cubing.

problems.stem: A tabletop is shaped like a trapezoid whose parallel sides measure $6$ feet and $10$ feet, with a distance of $4$ feet between them. What is the area, in square feet, of the tabletop?
steps: The distance between the parallel sides is the height, $h=4$.
problems.solution: "Distance between them" is the trapezoid's height, and both parallel sides must appear in the sum; using only one base gives $24$ or $20$, and forgetting the $\frac{1}{2}$ gives $64$. The area is $32$ square feet.

problems.figure: \begin{center}\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.32,line join=round] \draw[thick,satnavy] (0,0)--(20,0) arc (-90:90:5) -- (0,10) arc (90:270:5) -- cycle; \draw[dashed,satgrey] (0,0)--(0,10); \draw[dashed,satgrey] (20,0)--(20,10); \node[below] at (10,0) {$20$}; \node[right] at (20,5) {$10$}; \end{tikzpicture}\end{center}\satnote{Figure not drawn to scale.}
problems.stem: The region shown consists of a rectangle that is $20$ meters long and $10$ meters wide, with a semicircle attached to each of its two shorter sides. What is the area, in square meters, of the region?
steps: Each shorter side is $10$, so each semicircle has diameter $10$ and radius $5$.
The two semicircles together form one circle: $\pi(5)^2=25\pi$.
problems.solution: Two semicircles of equal radius combine into one full circle, and the side they sit on is a diameter, not a radius. Calling the radius $10$ gives $200+100\pi$ and counting two full circles gives $200+50\pi$; the area is $200+25\pi$ square meters.

problems.stem: A right circular cone has a volume of $96\pi$ cubic inches and a height of $8$ inches. What is the radius, in inches, of the cone's base?
problems.solution: Clearing the $\frac{1}{3}$ and the $\pi$ before touching $r$ keeps the arithmetic clean; forgetting the $\frac{1}{3}$ would give $r^2=12$ and no clean answer, which is a signal you dropped it. The radius is $6$ inches.
problems.verify:
r = symbols('r', positive=True)
result = solve(Eq(Rational(1,3)*pi*r**2*8, 96*pi), r)[0]

problems.stem: A closed cylindrical container has a base radius of $5$ centimeters and a height of $6$ centimeters. What is the total surface area, in square centimeters, of the container?
steps: The curved side unrolls into a rectangle of area $2\pi rh=2\pi(5)(6)=60\pi$.
problems.solution: A closed cylinder has three surfaces: two circles and one rolled-up rectangle whose width is the circumference. Using only the side gives $60\pi$ and counting one end gives $85\pi$; the total is $110\pi$ square centimeters.

problems.skill: Area and perimeter of plane figures
problems.stem: A rectangle has a perimeter of $34$ inches, and one of its sides has length $12$ inches. What is the area, in square inches, of the rectangle?
problems.solution: Half the perimeter is the sum of a length and a width, which is $17$, so the other side is $5$; the question then asks for the area, not that side. The area is $60$ square inches.
problems.verify:
w = symbols('w', positive=True)
ww = solve(Eq(2*(12+w), 34), w)[0]
result = 12*ww

problems.stem: A rectangular photograph with an area of $48$ square inches is enlarged so that each of its dimensions is multiplied by $2.5$. What is the area, in square inches, of the enlarged photograph?
problems.solution: Both dimensions grow, so the area grows by the square of the factor; multiplying $48$ by $2.5$ alone would answer for a single length. The enlarged area is $300$ square inches.

problems.stem: A solid consists of a right circular cylinder of radius $3$ inches and height $10$ inches with a hemisphere of radius $3$ inches attached to its top. What is the volume, in cubic inches, of the solid?
problems.solution: A composite solid is the sum of pieces you have formulas for, and a hemisphere is half a sphere: using a whole sphere gives $126\pi$ and using the diameter $6$ as the hemisphere's radius gives $234\pi$. The volume is $108\pi$ cubic inches.

problems.stem: A closed rectangular box measures $3$ inches by $4$ inches by $5$ inches. What is the minimum number of square inches of paper needed to cover the outside of the box exactly?
steps: The three distinct faces have areas $3\cdot 4=12$, $4\cdot 5=20$ and $3\cdot 5=15$.
problems.solution: Covering the outside asks for surface area, and a box has six faces in three matching pairs, so the sum $47$ must be doubled; $60$ is the volume, which is measured in cubic inches and cannot answer a question about paper. The answer is $94$ square inches.

problems.stem: A rectangular garden measures $15$ feet by $8$ feet. A walkway of uniform width $2$ feet is built around the outside of the garden. What is the area, in square feet, of the walkway alone?
steps: The walkway adds $2$ feet on each side, so the outer rectangle is $15+4=19$ by $8+4=12$.
problems.solution: A border of uniform width adds twice its width to each dimension, not once, and the walkway is the difference of the two rectangles. Treating it as perimeter times width gives $46\cdot 2=92$, which double-counts nothing and misses the four corners; the walkway covers $108$ square feet.

problems.figure: \begin{center}\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.5,line join=round] \draw[thick,satnavy] (0,0)--(6,0)--(8,2)--(2,2)--cycle; \draw[thick,satnavy] (0,0)--(4,6)--(6,0); \draw[thick,satnavy] (8,2)--(4,6); \draw[dashed,satgrey] (2,2)--(4,6); \draw[dashed,satgrey] (4,6)--(3,0); \node[below] at (3,0) {$6$}; \node[right] at (3.7,3) {$5$}; \end{tikzpicture}\end{center}\satnote{Figure not drawn to scale.}
problems.stem: A pyramid has a square base with edges of length $6$ centimeters. The slant height, measured from the apex to the midpoint of a base edge, is $5$ centimeters. What is the volume, in cubic centimeters, of the pyramid?
steps: The slant height, the vertical height, and half a base edge form a right triangle: $h^2+3^2=5^2$.
problems.solution: The slant height is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose other legs are the vertical height and half a base edge, so it can never go straight into the volume formula; using $5$ as the height gives $60$ and dropping the $\frac{1}{3}$ gives $144$. The volume is $48$ cubic centimeters.

problems.stem: Cylinder $A$ and cylinder $B$ are similar, and every length on cylinder $B$ is $3$ times the corresponding length on cylinder $A$. The volume of cylinder $A$ is $20$ cubic centimeters. What is the volume, in cubic centimeters, of cylinder $B$?
steps: Volumes of similar solids scale by $k^3$.
problems.solution: Similar means both the radius and the height are multiplied by $3$, and the volume formula multiplies three lengths, so the volume grows by $27$. Cylinder $B$ has volume $540$ cubic centimeters.

problems.stem: A sphere has a volume of $288\pi$ cubic units. What is the surface area, in square units, of the sphere?
problems.solution: The radius is the bridge between the two formulas: recover it from the volume, then feed it into the surface-area formula. Using the diameter $12$ as the radius gives $576\pi$, and the surface area is $144\pi$ square units.
problems.verify:
r = symbols('r', positive=True)
rr = solve(Eq(Rational(4,3)*pi*r**3, 288*pi), r)[0]
result = 4*pi*rr**2

problems.stem: Cylinder $P$ has radius $r$ and height $h$. Cylinder $Q$ has a radius half as long as cylinder $P$'s and a height twice as long as cylinder $P$'s. The volume of cylinder $Q$ is what fraction of the volume of cylinder $P$?
problems.solution: Halving and doubling do not cancel here, because the radius is squared and the height is not: the radius contributes $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{4}$ against the height's $2$. The volume of $Q$ is $\frac{1}{2}$ of the volume of $P$.
problems.verify:
r, h = symbols('r h', positive=True)
result = simplify((pi*(r/2)**2*(2*h))/(pi*r**2*h))

problems.stem: A rectangular prism has a square base, and its height is $4$ times the length of an edge of the base. The volume of the prism is $500$ cubic centimeters. What is the length, in centimeters, of an edge of the base?
steps: Let the base edge be $s$; the height is $4s$.
problems.solution: Writing every dimension in terms of one letter turns the volume into a single cubic equation; the height being a multiple of the base edge is what makes $s^3$ appear rather than $s^2$. The base edge is $5$ centimeters.
problems.verify:
s = symbols('s', positive=True)
result = solve(Eq(4*s**3, 500), s)[0]

problems.stem: A solid is formed by attaching a hemisphere of radius $3$ inches to the top of a right circular cylinder of radius $3$ inches and height $8$ inches, as shown. The bottom of the cylinder is a flat circular disk. What is the total surface area, in square inches, of the solid?
problems.solution: Count only the surfaces you could actually paint: the top circle of the cylinder is covered by the hemisphere, so it is not part of the outside, while the hemisphere adds half of a sphere's curved surface. Stopping at the cylinder alone gives $57\pi$ or $66\pi$; the total is $75\pi$ square inches.

problems.stem: Two similar right circular cones have volumes of $27$ cubic centimeters and $125$ cubic centimeters. The base radius of the smaller cone is $6$ centimeters. What is the base radius, in centimeters, of the larger cone?
steps: A radius is a length, so it scales by $k$: $6\cdot\frac{5}{3}=10$.
problems.solution: The ratio of volumes must be cube-rooted before it can be applied to a length; scaling the radius by $\frac{125}{27}$ instead would be the classic error. The larger cone's base radius is $10$ centimeters.
